title: Grade the biology, and get help
desc: Accommodations versus modifications, what to grade and what to let go, the state tests your students actually take, the Language Service Plan you're supposed to have a copy of, and the five people who can make your year easier.

cues.text: This is the last episode of Every Teacher, from EL Publishing. Marcus, biology. Elena, EL specialist. Episode six. Grading, testing, and help. Let's start with the question every teacher asks: do I grade an English learner the same as everybody else?

You grade the same standard. You don't grade the same way. There's a difference between an accommodation and a modification, and it's the most important distinction in this whole series. An accommodation changes how a student shows what they know. Extra time, a word bank, a bilingual dictionary, the question read aloud, answering by drawing instead of writing. The standard is the same. A modification changes the standard itself: fewer concepts, a lower-grade objective. English learners get accommodations, not modifications, unless there's a separate reason, like an I E P.
So a level one student is still responsible for understanding the cell.

Still responsible for the cell. Not responsible for writing an essay about the cell in English in September. Those are different things. The cell is content. The essay is language. You assess the content. You support the language.
How do I separate them when I'm grading a lab report?

Two rows on the rubric, or at least two questions in your head. Did they get the science right? Grade that fully. Was the English correct? Note it, give feedback on one thing, don't let it sink the grade. If a student writes, the water it was boil at one hundred degree, the science is right. That's full credit for science and a note about the verb. A student who gets a sixty because of their English will quit on you by October, and then you've lost the biology too.
Tests. My tests are mostly reading.

Most tests are mostly reading, which means most tests are testing English. A few things that keep a test fair without making it easier. Shorten the sentences in the questions. Put the question at the end of the word problem, not the middle. Use the same words you used in class. Allow a word-to-word dictionary. Let a level one answer by labeling or matching where you'd ask everyone else to write. And read the questions aloud if that's in the student's plan.
You mentioned the plan. The L S P.

The Language Service Plan. Every identified English learner in Mississippi has one. It says what level the student is in each domain, what services they get, and, this is the part that's about you, what accommodations each teacher provides in class and on tests. You are legally expected to provide those. It's usually one page of checkboxes. Get a copy. If it says extended time and a bilingual dictionary, that's not a suggestion. The good news is it's also a cheat sheet: somebody already figured out what this student needs, and wrote it down for you.
What about the state tests? What do my students actually take?

The same state tests as everybody else: the Biology test, Algebra one, English two, U S History, with the accommodations from their plan. Plus the E L P T every spring, which is the English test, and the one that moves them toward exiting. The thing to know is that nothing you do in class is wasted on the test. The five words, the sentence frames, the quick writes: that's exactly the language the E L P T measures. A biology teacher who runs ten minutes of structured talk a day is raising a student's speaking score without trying to.
That's a good way to think about it. Last thing. Who can help me? Because I didn't know you existed until October.

Five people. One, the EL teacher. We've got the scores, the plan, the leveled texts, and we will come co-teach a lesson if you ask. We'd rather be in your room than pulling the student out of it. Two, the counselor, for schedules, credits and the graduation path, which is complicated for a student who arrived at sixteen. Three, the family. Send the parent letter home in their language, and if there's a conference, ask for an interpreter. Don't use the student. Four, the other students. A rotating partner, a trained buddy, is the most underused resource in the building. And five, the student. Ask them what helps. A level three can tell you, in English, that the slides go too fast or that the word wall is the thing that saved them. They know. Nobody asks.
Give me the whole series in one minute.

Know your levels; pull the four domain scores. English in and English out, every day. Five words with pictures before you teach. Chunk your talk and show everything twice. Ten minutes of structured partner talk with frames. Preview the page, unpack one sentence, give a leveled version. Word bank, frame, model, then a two-minute quick write. Feedback on one thing. Grade the biology, not the English. Get the plan, provide the accommodations, and ask for help early. That's it. That's a year.
And the thing to stop worrying about, one last time.

Stop worrying that you're not doing enough. If the student in your room is understood and gets to speak every day, you're doing the most important thing a content teacher can do. The rest is practice.

Thank you, Elena. This has been Every Teacher, from EL Publishing.
